artworks.title: The Sleep of Endymion
artworks.description: Calyce, daughter of Aeolus, is rarely shown in her own right; her enduring place in art is as the mother of Endymion, the shepherd-king whose beauty led the Moon to love him. In this luminous Neoclassical canvas (Louvre, oil on canvas, 1.98 x 2.61 m), Girodet shows Calyce's son stretched in eternal sleep on Mount Latmos, his idealized body bathed not in a goddess's embrace but in a beam of silvered moonlight that parts the branches above him, while the winged Zephyr draws the foliage aside. The painting renders the destiny of Calyce's child as Apollodorus tells it: granted by Zeus the gift of his own choosing, Endymion chose to slumber forever, deathless and ageless, visited each night by the enamored Moon.

artworks.title: Selene and Endymion
artworks.description: This Venetian Rococo painting (Chiswick House, London; oil on canvas, 190 x 106 cm) depicts the central episode of the lineage Calyce founded: her son Endymion, lying asleep among the rocks of Caria, discovered by the Moon-goddess Selene, who descends from her chariot in a swirl of drapery and cloud to gaze upon the sleeping youth. Ricci stages the encounter with theatrical warmth, the goddess's luminous figure set against the dim hillside. The scene dramatizes the consequence of the union Apollodorus records between Calyce and Aethlius, whose surpassingly beautiful child became the immortal object of the Moon's nightly devotion.

artworks.title: Diana and Endymion
artworks.description: Exhibited at the Paris Salon of 1822, this large Neoclassical composition (oil on canvas, 318 x 211 cm) renders the Roman version of the myth, with the Moon in the guise of Diana leaning tenderly over the sleeping Endymion, son of Calyce. The towering canvas, signed and dated 'J. M. Langlois 1822,' presents the shepherd-king in idealized repose while the goddess, attended by Cupid, parts the night to reach him. As the descendant whose beauty defined his mother's fame, Endymion here embodies the legacy of Calyce's Aeolid line, which through her son Endymion led on to Aetolus and the Aetolian peoples.

artworks.title: Selene and Endymion (wall painting from the House of the Dioscuri, Pompeii)
artworks.description: This Fourth-Style Roman fresco from the triclinium of the House of the Dioscuri at Pompeii (now Museo Archeologico Nazionale, Naples, inv. 9240) shows Endymion, the son of Calyce, seated as a hunter on the rocks of a landscape, two spears in hand and a dog at his side, looking up as the Moon-goddess Selene descends toward him, with two female onlookers in the background. Among the earliest surviving depictions of the myth that carries Calyce's name into art, the painting attests how widely the story of her immortal sleeping son was loved across the ancient world, here decorating a wealthy Campanian household before the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 AD.
